ladder.title: Verb forms
ladder.intro: Danish verbs do not change with the person: jeg har, du har, vi har. They change with the time. This ladder practises the present, the past and the past participle.

notes.title: Hygge
claims: Hygge is a Danish and Norwegian word for a cozy, contented mood.
People use hygge, and forms made from it such as hyggelig, in both Denmark and Norway.
Hygge as a core part of Danish culture is a recent idea, from the late 20th century.
In Norway, hygge is just a word, much like “cozy”.
Meik Wiking wrote the Hygge Manifesto, which gives hygge ten ideals.
They include atmosphere, togetherness, comfort and shelter.

notes.title: The Law of Jante
claims: The Law of Jante is a made-up code of conduct.
Its name now describes disapproval of people who show off their personal success.
The author Aksel Sandemose invented it.
He first wrote it as ten rules in a novel from 1933.
The ten rules share one idea: you are not to think you are special.
People in Scandinavia often call it quintessentially Danish, Norwegian or Swedish.

notes.title: Smørrebrød
claims: Smørrebrød is an open sandwich from Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
The word first meant “butter and bread”.
It is a piece of buttered rugbrød, a dense, dark rye bread, with toppings.
Pickled herring is one traditional topping.
People usually eat it with a knife and fork.
At festive meals, fish toppings come first, then cold cuts and salads, then cheese.

notes.title: Hans Christian Andersen
claims: Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish writer.
He was born in Odense on 2 April 1805.
He is best remembered for his literary fairy tales.
His fairy tales have been translated into more than 125 languages.
They include “The Little Mermaid” and “The Nightingale”.
At 14 he moved to Copenhagen to look for work as an actor.

notes.title: The Danelaw
claims: The Danelaw was the part of England where Danish laws applied.
It began when Danish Vikings took large parts of eastern and northern England in the late ninth century.
The Great Heathen Army invaded England in 865.
In 867 the Danes captured York, which they called Jórvík.
The Danelaw covered about Yorkshire, the central and eastern Midlands, and the East of England.
The Danes kept their own laws and, in return, were loyal to England.
The meeting of the two cultures changed the language spoken in England.

notes.title: The Kalmar Union
claims: From 1397 to 1523, one monarch ruled Denmark, Sweden and Norway.
Queen Margaret I of Denmark designed the union.
The countries stayed separate states, but one monarch directed their policies.
Norway’s sea colonies, including Iceland, Greenland and the Faroe Islands, were part of the union too.
Nobles started it to counter the Hanseatic League, a northern German trade league.
Sweden left for good in 1523, when Gustav Vasa was elected its king.

notes.title: The constitution
claims: Denmark’s first democratic constitution was adopted in 1849.
It ended an absolute monarchy and brought in democracy.
The constitution in use now is from 1953.
Denmark is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system.
The parliament, the Folketing, cannot make laws that go against the constitution.
Denmark celebrates the constitution every year on 5 June.
It protects freedom of speech, religion, association and assembly.

notes.title: The rescue of the Danish Jews
claims: In the Second World War, the Danish resistance and many citizens took 7,500 of Denmark’s 8,000 Jews to Sweden.
On 28 September 1943, the German diplomat Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz leaked the German plan to arrest them.
The Danish state church and nearly every political party spoke out against the deportation.
It is seen as one of the largest acts of collective resistance in the countries Nazi Germany occupied.
As a result, 99 percent of Denmark’s Jewish population survived the Holocaust.

notes.title: The Danish language
claims: About 5.5 million people speak Danish, mostly in and around Denmark.
Danish is a North Germanic language.
It descends from Old Norse, the language of the Viking Era.
Speakers of Danish, Norwegian and Swedish largely understand one another, but not Icelandic or Faroese.
After the Reformation and the printing press, a standard Danish grew from the Copenhagen dialect.
Danish has a very large set of vowels: 27 that change meaning.

notes.title: Stød
claims: Stød is a feature of Danish sound. Its most common form is a kind of creaky voice.
In the IPA it is written with the sign ˀ.
The word stød itself does not have a stød.
A syllable with stød starts high and loud. Then the pitch and loudness drop.
Some word pairs differ only by stød, so it can change the meaning.
Gul, “yellow”, has stød. Its plural, gule, has none.
Two-syllable words with the accent on the first syllable have no stød.

notes.title: Danish sounds
claims: Spoken Danish can be hard for Norwegians and Swedes to understand, but they read it easily.
The sounds /p, t, k/ are said with a puff of air.
The sounds /b, d, g/ are said without that puff, so they sound like p, t and k.
Danish stop sounds are often called “lenis”: said with less muscle tension than in many languages.
The “soft d”, in Danish blødt d, is written ð in the IPA.

notes.title: Danish spelling
claims: The Danish alphabet has 29 letters, with three extra: æ, ø and å.
Writing and pronunciation do not match closely.
The Danish Language Council sets the spelling rules.
In 1948, the letter å replaced aa.
The 1948 reform ended capital letters on all nouns.
It also changed the past forms kunde, skulde and vilde to kunne, skulle and ville.

notes.title: En or et, and “the”
claims: Danish has two grammatical genders: common and neuter.
The word for “a” is en for common nouns and et for neuter nouns.
They are often called n-words and t-words.
En dreng is “a boy”, and et fængsel is “a jail”.
To say “the”, Danish adds a suffix to the noun. It does not add a separate word.
The suffix is -en for common nouns and -et for neuter nouns.
So drengen is “the boy” and fængslet is “the jail”.

notes.title: Danish numbers
claims: The numbers 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90 are built on twenty as a base.
French numbers from 80 to 99 work in a similar way.
Tres, 60, is short for tre-sinds-tyve, “three times twenty”.
Halvtreds, 50, is short for halvtredje-sinds-tyve, “two and a half times twenty”.
Today, 52 is usually said as tooghalvtreds.
